lessonData.subject: Mathematics / Geometry
lessonData.tagline: Pair up terms strategically to reveal hidden common factors and turn four terms into a clean product.
lessonData.overview: Factorisation by grouping is an algebraic strategy for four-term expressions where terms are split into pairs to extract common factors. By aligning the remaining binomial expressions—sometimes using sign adjustments like $(b - a) = -(a - b)$—the entire sum collapses neatly into a single product of two binomials.

diagram.title: The Four-Term Grouping Workflow
diagram.description: Follow the four logical stages from an expanded four-term expression to a fully factorised product.

nodes.label: Four-Term Expression
nodes.details: Identify an algebraic expression containing four terms with no single monomial factor common to all four.

nodes.label: Strategic Pairing
nodes.details: Group terms into two pairs that each share a common factor, rearranging term order if necessary.

nodes.label: Monomial Factoring
nodes.details: Extract the highest common factor from each pair to reveal binomial brackets.

nodes.label: Sign-Reversal Check
nodes.details: If the binomial brackets have opposite signs, factor out -1 from the second pair so the brackets match identically.

nodes.label: Binomial Extraction
nodes.details: Pull the common binomial bracket out front, leaving the combined monomial coefficients as the second factor.

chalkNotes.title: Factorisation by Grouping
chalkNotes.subtitle: Transforming 4 Terms into 2 Binomial Factors
chalkNotes.coreRuleOrFormula: ac + ad + bc + bd = (ac + ad) + (bc + bd) = a(c + d) + b(c + d) = (a + b)(c + d)
bulletPoints: Check first: Does a single common factor divide all four terms? If not, partition into two pairs of two terms.
Rearrange terms if your first pairing does not reveal any shared variables or coefficients.
Extract the HCF from each pair: both resulting brackets must match completely.
Sign Switch Identity: $(a - b) = -(b - a)$. If brackets differ only by signs, factor out a negative from the second group.
keyTakeaways: An expression is never fully factorised if there is still a '+' or '-' separating grouped terms; it must end as a single multiplication of brackets.
Always verify your answer by expanding the binomial factors using FOIL to recover the original expression.

quiz.question: A student factorises the expression 6x² - 9x + 15y - 10xy and arrives at the step: 3x(2x - 3) + 5y(3 - 2x). What is the correct next step to complete the factorisation fully?
options: The expression is already fully factorised because both pairs of terms have been factored
Multiply the brackets together to get 15xy(2x - 3)(3 - 2x)
Swap the signs inside the second bracket without changing the sign outside: 3x(2x - 3) + 5y(2x - 3)
quiz.explanation: Because (3 - 2x) and (2x - 3) are exact opposites, factor out -1: +5y(3 - 2x) becomes -5y(2x - 3). This aligns the brackets, permitting the extraction of the common binomial (2x - 3) to yield (2x - 3)(3x - 5y). Leaving the expression with a '+' between terms is an incomplete factorisation, and signs cannot be flipped inside brackets without balancing the sign outside.

suggestedQuestions: Diagnostic check: How do I factorise a single pair like 12ax - 8bx before attempting grouping?
What should I do if my chosen grouping gives brackets that share no common terms at all?
Why is leaving an answer as a(c + d) + b(c + d) considered an incomplete factorisation?

factorisation-by-grouping.title: Factorisation by Grouping Process
factorisation-by-grouping.description: A step-by-step workflow showing how to factorise a four-term polynomial by grouping terms into pairs.

nodes.label: Four-Term Polynomial
nodes.details: Start with four algebraic terms that do not share a single common factor across all terms.

nodes.label: Group into Pairs
nodes.details: Rearrange and split the polynomial into two separate pairs that each share common factors.

nodes.label: Extract GCF from Pairs
nodes.details: Factor out the greatest common monomial from each pair to reveal an identical binomial factor.

nodes.label: Extract Common Binomial
nodes.details: Factor out the matching bracketed binomial (x + y) to write the expression as a complete product.

key-properties-of-factorisation-by-group.title: Key Properties of Factorisation by Grouping
key-properties-of-factorisation-by-group.description: Essential structural rules and sequential properties needed to factorise algebraic expressions by grouping terms.

nodes.label: Four-Term Structure
nodes.details: Requires an even number of terms, most commonly four, with no single common factor across all terms.

nodes.label: Pairwise Common Factors
nodes.details: Terms are rearranged into pairs where each separate pair yields its own highest common factor (HCF).

nodes.label: Identical Binomial Factor
nodes.details: Both grouped pairs must reveal the exact same binomial factor inside the parentheses, adjusting signs if necessary.

nodes.label: Product of Binomials
nodes.details: The shared binomial is factored out as a single unit, leaving a fully factorised product of two binomials.

main.title: Factorisation by Grouping
main.why: This grid shows how grouping terms allows us to factor out a common binomial, revealing that the expression is the area of a rectangle with sides (a+b) and (c+d).
main.checkQuestion: If I change the expression to (ac + ad) + (bc + bd), how do the labels (a+b) and (c+d) describe the total area?

steps.name: Draw the rectangle
steps.caption: Imagine the expression as the area of a rectangle made of four parts.

steps.name: Add divisions
steps.caption: Split the rectangle to see how we group pairs of terms together.

steps.name: Label sides
steps.caption: The common factors of each row and column form the new dimensions.

steps.name: Final product
steps.caption: Factorising changes the sum of parts into a product of two factors.

contrast:stop-at-partial-grouping.title: Full Factorisation vs Partial
contrast:stop-at-partial-grouping.why: It shows that an expression with an addition sign between terms is not a product, making the difference between partial and full factorisation visually clear.
contrast:stop-at-partial-grouping.checkQuestion: Is an expression fully factorised if there is still an addition sign between the terms?

steps.name: Partial Step
steps.caption: Here is the result after grouping and extracting common factors from each pair.

steps.name: Complete Step
steps.caption: We can factor out the common bracket (3a - 2b) to finish the job.

steps.name: Check Question
steps.caption: Look at the two results: why does the bottom expression count as 'factorised' while the top does not?

contrast:stop-at-partial-grouping.focus: Grouping terms that do not share a common binomial factor, and stopping halfway, e.g. leaving an answer as $a(c+d) + bc + bd$.

contrast:opposite-sign-bracket-confusion.title: Unlocking the Bracket Sign
contrast:opposite-sign-bracket-confusion.why: It shows that multiplying a binomial by -1 physically flips the signs inside, enabling a match between bracketed terms.
contrast:opposite-sign-bracket-confusion.checkQuestion: Looking at the transition in the third step, how did multiplying by -1 change the signs inside the bracket to match the first one?

steps.name: The mismatch
steps.caption: When we group, sometimes the signs inside the brackets are reversed.

steps.name: Testing the flip
steps.caption: What happens when we multiply (3 - 2x) by -1?

steps.name: Substitution
steps.caption: Now both brackets match, allowing us to factor them out.

steps.name: Final result
steps.caption: We have successfully factorised the expression into two identical binomial factors.

contrast:opposite-sign-bracket-confusion.focus: Failing to recognize that $(a - b) = -(b - a)$.

apply.title: Factorisation by Grouping Application
apply.why: The visual grid structure forces the learner to organize terms into groups and identify common factors along the edges.
apply.checkQuestion: How can you arrange these four terms into pairs within the grid to reveal a common binomial factor?

steps.name: Present the expression
steps.caption: Let's factorise this four-term expression by using a 2x2 grid.

steps.name: Draw the grid
steps.caption: Place the four terms into the grid cells to prepare for grouping.

3d.title: Factorisation by Grouping: The Area Model
3d.why: Students often struggle to see why grouping results in a product; the area model shows the expression as the total area of four rectangular tiles that combine into one large rectangle.
3d.checkQuestion: If you factorise ac + ad + bc + bd, why must the (c + d) terms match exactly?

steps.name: Visualize the four terms
steps.caption: Imagine these four terms as areas of four smaller rectangles.

steps.name: Group by shared side
steps.caption: We group them by common sides: 'a' is common to the top pair, 'b' to the bottom.

steps.name: Factor out the common side
steps.caption: Factoring out 'a' and 'b' gives us two new rectangles: a(c+d) and b(c+d).

steps.name: Combine the factors
steps.caption: Finally, we see the total area is (a+b) multiplied by (c+d).
